title: The mango given at the door
hookLine: two mangoes, a hungry devotee of Shiva at the door, and a husband who wants the second one
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is God
tomorrow: The boy who answered with a song

lines: ONE GOES TO A HUNGRY GUEST.
cards: Two mangoes arrive at a merchant's house in the port town of Karaikkal. The merchant sent them home for his lunch. His wife, Punitavati, puts them aside.
Then a knock: a wandering devotee of Shiva, worn out and hungry. She has rice but nothing to go with it, so she gives him rice and one of the mangoes. He eats, blesses her, and goes.
Then her husband comes home, eats the remaining mango, loves it, and says: bring me the other one.

teach.h: A MANGO APPEARS IN HER HAND.
teach.b: The Periya Puranam tells it like this. Punitavati goes into the kitchen and prays to Shiva, and a mango appears in her hand. It's so sweet her husband asks where it came from, and she tells him the truth.
Then get me another, he says. She prays again, another mango appears, and the moment he takes it, it vanishes. Now he's afraid.
So he quietly sails away on business, settles in another town, marries again, and names his daughter Punitavati. Punitavati doesn't ask for him back.
She asks Shiva to take away the beauty she kept for her husband and give her the form of a pey, a gaunt, ghost-like being.
She sets out for Shiva's mountain and, the Periya Puranam says, goes up on her head, so her feet won't touch the holy ground.
Shiva sees her coming and calls her Mother. She's Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother of Karaikkal. Now look at where it all began: a mango given to a hungry stranger.
Not just any stranger: a devotee of Shiva. For the Nayanars, serving Shiva's devotees was serving Shiva himself.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.
teach.b: Behind it is an old Hindu teaching, in the Taittiriya Upanishad's words: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be God to you.

It's why so many Hindu grandmothers won't let anyone leave unfed, and why the guest is so often served first. Punitavati fed the guest before her husband, and the story says Shiva himself filled her hand.

how: Karaikkal Ammaiyar is honored among the Nayanars in Shiva temples, and in Karaikkal a mango festival remembers the story of the two mangoes.

o: the ghostly dancers of Shiva's cremation ground
the Tamil saints of Shiva, told in the Periya Puranam
merchants of Karaikkal who give food to pilgrims

games.q: the mango story — tap the pairs.
p: let the guest be God to you

s: Punitavati asked Shiva to bring her husband back
she asked for her beauty to be taken away, and the form of a pey.
she went up Shiva's mountain on her head
upside down, so her feet wouldn't touch the holy ground.
for the Nayanars, feeding a devotee of Shiva was just a small kindness
serving Shiva's devotees was serving Shiva himself. the guest is God.

games.q: you're Punitavati. two mangoes are set aside for your husband's lunch, and a hungry devotee of Shiva knocks. you have plain rice. what fits the story?
o: save the mangoes; your husband comes first.
give the guest rice and a mango: the guest is God.
give him rice only; mangoes are a luxury.
games.why: she gives him rice and a mango. for the Nayanars, Shiva's devotee at the door was Shiva himself, and the story says Shiva filled her hand again.

practice: Picture your front door, and someone knocking who needs something small. Notice the voice that says save it for later; just breathe beside it. Then say quietly, atithi devo bhava, the guest is God.
If you pray, pray to Shiva, or in words you already know, for whoever may knock on your door this week. If you don't pray, choose one person you'll serve first this week, before yourself.

wordCard.voice: The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva, who served his devotees as they would serve Shiva. Karaikkal Ammaiyar is the woman of the mangoes, whom Shiva called Mother.

orig.note: Tamil: the mother of Karaikkal, the name given to Punitavati.
